notes.meaning: Joshua called together the soldiers of Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh. The major battles in Canaan were now finished, and the western tribes had received their allotments. Joshua formally gathered these eastern fighters to release them with honor from their military service.

Joshua praised these eastern tribes for keeping every promise they had made. They obeyed the commands Moses gave them before he died, and they followed Joshua's orders without hesitation throughout the campaign. Their faithful obedience earned them great respect.

For years of hard fighting, these soldiers never abandoned their fellow Israelites. They stayed away from their own families across the river until the other tribes were settled. They fulfilled their duty to their brothers and remained faithful to God.

The Lord had fulfilled His promise by giving the western tribes rest from their enemies. With that work complete, Joshua told the eastern soldiers they were finally free to return to their homes. They could now enjoy the land Moses had assigned them east of the Jordan River.

Joshua gave them an urgent warning before sending them away. He told them to love the Lord, walk in His paths, hold close to Him, and obey His law with all their heart and soul. Outward victory would mean nothing if they lost their inner devotion to God.

Joshua blessed the departing tribes and sent them on their way. He prayed for God's protection and favor over them and their households. The soldiers then began their journey back to their settled homes.

The writer reminds readers that Moses gave land east of the Jordan to one half of the tribe of Manasseh, while Joshua gave land on the west side to the other half. Joshua gave a special parting blessing to the eastern half-tribe as they departed. Even though they lived on opposite sides of the river, both halves were part of the same family.

Joshua told the soldiers to go home with their share of the wealth taken from the defeated nations. This included large herds of animals, silver, gold, bronze, iron, and fine clothing. He commanded them to divide these goods with the men who had stayed behind to guard their families and farms.

The eastern tribes packed their belongings and left the main camp at Shiloh in Canaan. They headed eastward toward their home territory of Gilead. They were returning to possess the land the Lord had promised them through Moses.

When the eastern tribes reached the Jordan valley, they stopped and built a massive stone altar near the river. It was built tall and wide so that anyone passing by could see it. They intended it as a memorial, but its large size soon caused great alarm.

Word quickly traveled back to the western tribes that an altar had been erected near the border. Because God commanded Israel to bring sacrifices to only one central place, the western tribes suspected the worst. They feared their brothers were setting up an unlawful rival worship site.

The whole assembly of western Israel gathered at Shiloh, ready to march to war against their eastern brothers. God's law required them to purge idolatry and false worship from the land. Their swift reaction showed a deep passion for keeping Israel pure before the Lord.

Before attacking, the western tribes acted wisely by sending an official group to investigate the matter. They chose Phinehas, the son of the high priest Eleazar, to lead the delegation. Phinehas was well known for his courage and his deep passion for God's holiness.

Ten leading rulers joined Phinehas, one representing each of the western tribes. These men were respected heads of families across the nation. Sending such high-ranking leaders showed how seriously the whole country took the situation.

The delegation crossed the river into Gilead to meet with the leaders of the eastern tribes. They came to confront them directly and hear the truth before any blood was shed. A peaceful hearing gave both sides a chance to speak.

Speaking for the whole nation, the leaders asked why the eastern tribes were turning away from God. They assumed the new altar was meant for unauthorized sacrifices, which would be direct rebellion against the Lord. They viewed building a second altar as breaking faith with the God who had saved them.

Phinehas reminded them of the tragic sin at Peor, where many Israelites had worshipped a false god and died in a plague. He warned that the nation was still carrying the stain and sorrow of that rebellion. He asked if that past disaster was not enough to teach them to remain faithful.

The delegation warned that rebelling against God today would bring His anger on the entire nation tomorrow. Because all the tribes were bound together in God's covenant, one group's sin could bring suffering to everyone. They pleaded with their brothers not to put the whole community at risk.

The western leaders made a remarkably generous offer to their brothers. If the eastern tribes felt their land was somehow unholy without a tabernacle, they were invited to move across the river and share Canaan. The western tribes were willing to give up some of their own property to keep their brothers from falling into sin.

Phinehas pointed to the tragic story of Achan, who stole forbidden items from Jericho and brought God's anger upon the whole army. Achan did not die alone; other innocent soldiers lost their lives because of his wrongdoing. The leaders argued that if one man's hidden sin caused such grief, an entire region in rebellion would destroy the nation.

The eastern leaders listened quietly until the western princes finished their severe accusations. Then they stepped forward to give their response to the rulers of Israel. They remained calm and respectful instead of responding with anger.

The eastern tribes began with a passionate confession of faith, repeating the holy names of God to show their absolute loyalty to Him. They appealed to the Lord, who knows all hearts, to judge their real intentions. They stated that if they had acted in rebellion, they deserved to be put to death immediately.

They insisted they never intended to use the altar for burnt offerings, grain offerings, or peace offerings. They fully agreed that making sacrifices outside the tabernacle was wrong. They asked the Lord Himself to punish them if they were lying.

The eastern tribes explained that deep fear, not pride, had motivated them to build the altar. They worried about the future when their children grew up across the river. They feared western descendants might someday tell eastern children that they had no right to worship Israel's God.

The Jordan River was a wide, natural boundary that separated the land into two halves. The eastern tribes feared that geographic separation would eventually cause spiritual separation. If their children were excluded from the community, they might stop revering and worshipping the Lord altogether.

To prevent that future danger, they decided to construct a large replica of the Lord's altar. They stressed again that it was never designed for burning animal sacrifices or bringing gifts. It was built strictly as a visual sign for future generations.

The stone structure was meant to serve as an enduring witness between both sides of the river. It would prove that the eastern tribes had the right to travel to the tabernacle at Shiloh to present their offerings before God's presence. That way, no one in the future could ever claim they had no part in the Lord.

If future generations ever challenged their right to worship, their descendants could point to this exact copy of the tabernacle altar. Its shape and design would show that their ancestors worshipped the same God and respected the true altar at Shiloh. The replica was proof of unity, not division.

The eastern leaders stated plainly that they had no desire to rebel against the Lord or corrupt His worship. They affirmed that only one altar was authorized for sacrifice, the one standing in front of the tabernacle. They completely agreed with the biblical principle that the western tribes were defending.

Phinehas and the ten tribal rulers were completely satisfied once they heard the full story. Their anger cooled because they saw their brothers were acting out of love for God, not rebellion. They gladly accepted the explanation without holding onto their earlier suspicions.

Phinehas declared that God's favor was clearly resting on them because no sin had actually occurred. Because the eastern tribes were innocent of rebellion, the whole nation was spared from God's wrath and a bloody civil war. Good communication had saved God's people from a terrible disaster.

Phinehas and the rulers traveled back across the Jordan River to Canaan. They gave a thorough report to the assembly of Israel, explaining what the eastern tribes had said. They cleared their brothers of every charge.

The Israelites in Canaan were relieved and joyful when they heard the good news. They praised God for keeping their brothers faithful and dropped all plans to attack them. What could have been a tragic civil war ended in worship and renewed unity.

The eastern tribes gave the altar a name that meant 'Witness.' It stood as a permanent reminder to both sides of the river that the Lord alone is God. That massive heap of stones testified that all twelve tribes served the same God in peace.
